title: The Chaubole verses

lines: WHAT WOULD YOU PAY FOR LOVE?
cards: What would you pay for love? It's an odd question until someone actually tries. A ring that costs too much.
A trip meant to fix things. A gift that arrives instead of a person. On Ang thirteen hundred sixty-three, just past the Funhe, Guru Arjan's Chaubole take up that question.
They speak of love, calling out to listeners by name. And the first thing they say is about money, and what it can't do.

teach.b: The name is often heard as chau, four, and bole, things spoken: four sayings, or four voices. Readers explain the four in different ways, and the text doesn't stop to say.
What's clear is the subject: love, prem, the love of the soul for the Lord.
The verses call out to people by name, Samman and Musan among them, as if the Guru were turning to friends in a circle. Here's one, paraphrased.
Samman, if this love could be bought with money, think of Ravan, the king of the old epic. He was no pauper, the verse says, and he gave his own heads, yet he could not buy it.
That's the turn: a king with treasure to spare, willing to give even his own heads, still couldn't purchase it. Love of this kind isn't a sale.
Other verses, paraphrased again, speak of love spread like moonlight across the sky, and of the bumblebee caught fast in the lotus it loves.

teach.h: LOVE FROM MORE THAN ONE SIDE.
teach.b: Four voices can also mean something simple and human: love gets talked about from more than one side.
The one who longs, the one who's asked, the friend who watches, the Beloved who's silent. One voice would make it a lecture.
Several make it a conversation, and it keeps coming back to the same discovery: what the soul wants most can't be bought, only given and received.

how: Guru Arjan's Chaubole are read among the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib; gianis may explain them in katha, including the verse about a love that money cannot buy.

o: a hymn sung by four singers taking turns at the gurdwara
Guru Arjan's verses on love, often heard as four sayings
four rules for a Sikh wedding, read before the vows

games.q: inside the Chaubole: tap the pairs.
p: a name the verses call out to
rich, yet couldn't buy this love

s: the Chaubole say love can be bought by someone rich enough
Ravan was no pauper and gave his own heads, the verse says, yet he could not buy it.
the Chaubole call out to listeners by name
they speak to Samman and Musan among others, like friends in a circle.

games.q: you're Ravan, king of the old epic, wealthy beyond counting. you want this love, the love of the soul for the Lord. what happens when you try to pay?
o: you buy it, because you can afford anything.
you give even your own heads, and still can't buy it.
you get half of it for half the price.
games.why: the verse uses a king with treasure to spare to show that this love isn't a sale; it can only be given and received.

practice: If you can find the Chaubole on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-three, read one verse and notice who it's speaking to.

If not, hold someone you love in mind and let four voices take a turn in silence: what you'd say to them, what they might say back, what a friend watching would say, and the quiet underneath. Then let the breath settle.
